questions.question: Which implication between strong and topological equivalence of metrics is valid?
options: Topological equivalence always implies strong equivalence.
Topological equivalence implies the metrics are identical functions.
No two distinct metrics can be topologically equivalent.
Strong equivalence of metrics implies topological equivalence.

questions.question: What does the discrete-metric example show about topological equivalence with the usual $p$-metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: The discrete metric is not topologically equivalent to the usual $p$-metrics.
The discrete metric is topologically but not strongly equivalent to the $p$-metrics.
The discrete metric is strongly, hence topologically, equivalent to the $p$-metrics.
The discrete metric is topologically equivalent to them, as both make singletons closed.

questions.question: If a sequence convergence statement is based only on open sets and two metrics are topologically equivalent, which expectation is natural?
options: It should be unchanged under replacing one metric by the other.
It can change, since the two metrics measure distances differently.
It is unchanged only if the metrics are also strongly equivalent.
Convergence is kept, but the limit may become a different point.

questions.question: Two metrics $d_p$ and $d_q$ on a set $X$ are topologically equivalent, $d_p\sim d_q$, exactly when which condition holds?
options: $d_p(x,y)=d_q(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$.
Every open ball for $d_p$ is also an open ball for $d_q$, with the same centre and radius.
A subset of $X$ is open for $d_p$ if and only if it is open for $d_q$.
Every subset of $X$ that is open for $d_p$ is also open for $d_q$.

questions.question: Let $d_p\sim d_q$ be topologically equivalent metrics on $X$, let $E\subseteq X$ and let $(x_n)$ be a sequence in $X$. Which property can hold with respect to $d_p$ but fail with respect to $d_q$?
options: $E$ is open.
$E$ is closed.
$E$ is bounded.
$(x_n)$ converges to the point $x\in X$.

questions.question: Which pair of metrics on the stated space is topologically equivalent but not strongly equivalent?
options: $d_1$ and $d_2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$.
The discrete metric and $|x-y|$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
$|\tan x-\tan y|$ and $|x-y|$ on $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$.
$|x-y|$ and $2|x-y|$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: Which condition captures topological equivalence of two metrics $d_p$ and $d_q$ on $X$?
options: A subset $E\subseteq X$ is bounded with respect to $d_p$ precisely when it is bounded with respect to $d_q$.
A subset $E\subseteq X$ is open with respect to $d_p$ precisely when it is closed with respect to $d_q$.
A subset $E\subseteq X$ is open with respect to $d_p$ precisely when it is open with respect to $d_q$.
There are $a,b>0$ with $a\,d_p(x,y)\le d_q(x,y)\le b\,d_p(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$.

questions.question: Let $d_p$ and $d_q$ be metrics on a set $X$, with open balls $B_d(x,r)=\{y\in X\colon d(x,y)<r\}$. Which condition on balls is equivalent to $d_p\sim d_q$, i.e. to $d_p$ and $d_q$ having the same open sets?
options: For all $x\in X$ and $r>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $B_{d_q}(x,\delta)\subseteq B_{d_p}(x,r)$.
There is one $c>0$ with $B_{d_q}(x,cr)\subseteq B_{d_p}(x,r)$ and $B_{d_p}(x,cr)\subseteq B_{d_q}(x,r)$ for all $x\in X$, $r>0$.
For all $x\in X$ and $r>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $B_{d_q}(x,\delta)\subseteq B_{d_p}(x,r)$ and $B_{d_p}(x,\delta)\subseteq B_{d_q}(x,r)$.
For all $x\in X$ and $r>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $B_{d_q}(x,\delta)\supseteq B_{d_p}(x,r)$ and $B_{d_p}(x,\delta)\supseteq B_{d_q}(x,r)$.

questions.question: For a subset $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, compare the metric $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ restricted to $X$ with the discrete metric on $X$. For which $X$ are these two metrics topologically equivalent?
options: $X=\mathbb{Q}$
$X=\{0\}\cup\{\frac{1}{n}\colon n\geq1\text{ an integer}\}$
$X=\mathbb{Z}$
